prompt: When decomposing the Level 0 DFD of an ATM system into a Level 1 DFD for 'Withdraw Cash', the analyst ensures every input and output shown for 'Withdraw Cash' at Level 0 is still accounted for among the Level 1 sub-processes. Which two statements describe this practice and its purpose?

options.text: This practice is called gray-holing
Its purpose is to eliminate the need for a context diagram
This practice is called balancing
Its purpose is to ensure consistency between the parent process and its decomposed sub-processes

explanation: BALANCING is the rule that a child diagram must show exactly the same net inputs and outputs as the parent process it explodes. Nothing may appear from nowhere and nothing may vanish. It is what keeps a set of levelled diagrams describing ONE system rather than several, and it is the first thing an examiner checks when you hand in a Level 1 diagram.

why.a: Wrong. A gray hole is a DEFECT, a process whose outputs cannot be produced from its inputs, not a good practice.
why.b: Wrong. The context diagram is the Level 0 boundary view and is still needed.
why.c: Correct. This is the definition of balancing.
why.d: Correct. Consistency between parent and children is exactly what balancing guarantees.

prompt: In a Data Flow Diagram, which symbol represents "data at rest," as opposed to "data in motion"?

options.text: Data flow
Process
Data store
External agent

explanation: Four symbols, and this pair of phrases separates two of them cleanly. A DATA FLOW is data in MOTION, an arrow carrying data from one place to another. A DATA STORE is data at REST, data held so it can be used later. If the data is going somewhere it is a flow; if it is sitting somewhere it is a store.

why.a: Wrong, and it is the exact opposite: a data flow is data in motion.
why.b: Wrong. A process TRANSFORMS data; it does not hold it.
why.c: Correct. A store holds data at rest.
why.d: Wrong. An external agent sits outside the system boundary and supplies or receives data.

prompt: Match each fact-finding technique with its core definition.

pairs.right: Systems analyst participates in or watches a person performing job activities to learn about the system firsthand

pairs.left: Sampling of existing documentation, forms and databases
pairs.right: Reviewing organisation charts, memos, forms, reports and databases to understand current business rules and processes
Building a small-scale, representative or working model of requirements so users can interact with it and give feedback
Special-purpose document used to collect information and opinions from many respondents quickly and at low cost
Highly structured group meetings conducted to analyse problems and define requirements

explanation: Five techniques, and the quickest way to hold them apart is to ask WHO is in the room and WHAT is being examined. Observation watches one person working. Sampling reads documents rather than talking to anyone. Discovery prototyping shows a model and collects reactions. Questionnaires reach many people cheaply but shallowly. JRP puts everyone in one highly structured meeting.

prompt: An analyst wants a department head to describe the credit-approval process in his own words rather than following a rigid script, while she keeps only one overarching topic in mind for the session. Which two features characterise the interview approach she is using?

options.text: The interviewer relies on the interviewee to help direct the conversation
It is conducted with only a general goal or subject in mind
It uses a specific, fixed set of questions prepared in advance
It restricts every response to a predefined set of choices

explanation: This is the UNSTRUCTURED interview. It is conducted with only a general goal in mind and lets the interviewee steer, which is exactly what you want when you do not yet know enough to write good questions. Its opposite, the structured interview, uses a fixed set of prepared questions and is better once you know what to ask.

why.a: Correct. Letting the interviewee direct the conversation is the defining feature.
why.b: Correct. A general goal or subject rather than a script.
why.c: Wrong. A fixed prepared set of questions describes the STRUCTURED interview.
why.d: Wrong. Restricting responses to set choices describes a closed-ended question or a questionnaire.

prompt: Which of the following correctly describes the arrow direction convention for an extends relationship, such as "Generate Warehouse Packing Order" extending "Place New Member Order"?

options.text: The arrow is drawn from the extension use case to the use case being extended, labelled with the extends stereotype
The arrow is drawn from the base use case to the extension use case, labelled with the extends stereotype
The arrow is drawn from the extension use case to the actor, labelled with the include stereotype
No arrow is used; extends relationships are shown only as dashed rectangles

explanation: EXTENDS points from the extension BACK to the base, which feels backwards until you read it as a sentence: "Generate Warehouse Packing Order EXTENDS Place New Member Order". The arrow follows the sentence. Contrast INCLUDES, which points from the base to the thing it always uses: "Place New Member Order INCLUDES Check Credit". Get the two directions straight and this whole family of questions falls.

why.a: Correct. From the extension to the base, with the extends stereotype.
why.b: Wrong direction. That is how INCLUDES is drawn.
why.c: Wrong twice: the arrow does not point at an actor, and the stereotype is extends, not include.
why.d: Wrong. It is a dashed arrow with a stereotype label, not a rectangle.

prompt: Which of the following most accurately describes why DFDs are described as "purely logical, not physical models"?

options.text: Because they can only be drawn using computer-aided software engineering tools
Because they represent the physical wiring and network topology of the system's servers
Because they capture what the organisation does and how it processes data without specifying implementation details such as programming languages or hardware
Because they must always be paired with a corresponding entity-relationship diagram before they can be considered valid

explanation: A logical model says WHAT happens; a physical model says HOW it is built. A DFD names the processes, the data that moves between them and the stores it rests in, and says nothing about the language, the database product or the servers. That is deliberate: it lets you agree the business behaviour with users who neither know nor care what it will be written in.

why.a: Wrong. The tool used to draw it has nothing to do with whether the model is logical.
why.b: Wrong, and it is the opposite: wiring and topology are exactly the physical detail a DFD leaves out.
why.c: Correct. What the organisation does, without implementation detail.
why.d: Wrong. A DFD is valid on its own, though the two models are often drawn together.

prompt: A DFD process labelled "Create a new member account" shows inputs of "Membership application" and "Existing account" but has no outgoing data flow at all. This situation is best classified as which type of error?

options.text: A balancing violation
A gray hole
A miracle
A black hole

explanation: Three named process errors, and the pictures are worth remembering. A BLACK HOLE takes data in and lets none out, so data disappears. A MIRACLE produces output from no input, so data appears from nowhere. A GRAY HOLE has both, but the inputs are not enough to produce the stated outputs. Here data goes in and nothing comes out, so it is a black hole.

why.a: Wrong. Balancing concerns consistency BETWEEN levels, not one process on one diagram.
why.b: Wrong. A gray hole does produce output, just not output the inputs could justify.
why.c: Wrong, and reversed: a miracle has output with no input.
why.d: Correct. Inputs but no outputs at all: data goes in and never comes out.

prompt: According to requirements discovery theory, a "problem" in the context of requirements discovery is best defined as which of the following?

options.text: A defect discovered exclusively during the system testing phase
Any deviation from the originally approved project schedule
A disagreement between two stakeholders about a user-interface colour scheme
An undesirable situation that prevents the organisation from fully achieving its mission, vision, goals, and objectives

explanation: Notice how wide this definition is. A problem is anything standing between the organisation and its mission, vision, goals and objectives. It is not restricted to bugs, or to lateness, or to anything technical at all. That breadth is the point: it is why the analyst starts with the business rather than the software.

why.a: Wrong, and far too narrow. Testing defects are one small kind of problem.
why.b: Wrong. Schedule slippage is a project management issue, not the definition.
why.c: Wrong. A preference disagreement is not an obstacle to the mission.
why.d: Correct. An undesirable situation preventing the organisation achieving its mission, vision, goals and objectives.

prompt: In the 'Order Glasses' use-case diagram, the Patient actor interacts with 'Get Prescription', 'Select Frame', 'Place Order', 'Make Payment', and 'Fitting and Adjustment'. Before finalising the diagram, the analyst checks her actor identification. Which two questions did she likely use to confirm the Patient qualifies as an actor?

options.text: Which internal process transforms input data into output data?
Who or what provides input to the system?
Who or what receives output from the system?
Are there any events automatically triggered at a predetermined time within the store's internal database?

explanation: An actor is defined by sitting OUTSIDE the system and exchanging something with it, so the two identifying questions are about input and output across the boundary. A patient supplies a prescription and a payment, and receives glasses and a fitting, so on both counts the Patient is an actor.

why.a: Wrong. An internal transformation is a PROCESS, and processes are inside the boundary, which is what actors are not.
why.b: Correct. Who or what provides input is one of the two identifying questions.
why.c: Correct. Who or what receives output is the other.
why.d: Wrong. That describes a TIME or temporal event, which can be an actor in some notations but is not how a patient was identified.

prompt: An analyst drafts a DFD in which data flows directly from the 'Employees' data store to the 'Accounts Receivable Department' external entity, without passing through any process. Which two statements correctly evaluate this design?

options.text: No correction is needed because data stores are considered a type of process in Gane-Sarson notation
A process is needed to retrieve and present the data from the store to the external agent
This is an illegal data flow because an external agent cannot access a data store directly
This is a legal data flow because data stores may output directly to any external agent that needs the information

explanation: The rule is simple and the examiner leans on it: EVERY data flow must touch at least one process. A store cannot talk to an external agent, a store cannot talk to another store, and an agent cannot talk to another agent, all for the same reason: nothing would be doing any work. Something has to retrieve the data and present it, and that something is a process.

why.a: Wrong. A data store is not a process in any notation; they are separate symbols with separate rules.
why.b: Correct. A process must retrieve and present the data.
why.c: Correct. Store to external agent with no process between is an illegal flow.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the misconception the question is testing.

prompt: Match each use-case narrative element with its definition.

pairs.right: Conditions that must be true before the use case can begin
The step-by-step sequence of actions between actor and system when everything works correctly
Describes variations, exceptions, or error situations that branch off the main flow
Describes what must be true after the use case has completed

explanation: Read them as a story with a before and an after. PRECONDITIONS are what must already be true to start. The MAIN FLOW is the happy path, where nothing goes wrong. ALTERNATIVE FLOWS are the branches for exceptions and errors. POSTCONDITIONS are what is true once it is over. Pre and post are the bookends; main and alternative are the story between them.

prompt: While reviewing personnel files during fact-finding for a new HR system, an analyst discovers detailed salary and medical history information about several employees. Which two actions are consistent with the stated fact-finding ethics for systems analysts?

options.text: Refrain from using the sensitive information for any purpose beyond the project
Use the medical history information to make personal judgements about employee reliability
Take steps to protect the sensitive information from people who might misuse it
Share interesting salary details informally with curious colleagues

explanation: Two duties, and they are the two halves of confidentiality. The first is about YOU: do not use what you learn for anything outside the project. The second is about EVERYONE ELSE: actively protect it from people who might misuse it. Access granted for a purpose is limited to that purpose, and protecting it is a duty rather than a courtesy.

why.a: Correct. Use it only for the project it was given for.
why.b: Wrong, and it is precisely the misuse the ethics forbid.
why.c: Correct. Actively protect it from misuse by others.
why.d: Wrong. Informal sharing is a breach however casual it feels.

prompt: According to the rules for constructing a Context Diagram (Process 0), which of the following is generally true?

options.text: The Context Diagram must show every sub-process contained within the system
The Context Diagram is drawn only after all Level 1 DFDs have been completed
Data stores are usually excluded unless they are owned by systems or processes other than the one being documented
Data stores must always be shown explicitly, regardless of ownership

explanation: A context diagram shows the system as ONE process and draws the boundary around it. Everything inside is hidden, so internal data stores do not appear. The exception is a store the system does not own, belonging to some other system, because that is genuinely outside the boundary and the flow to it has to be shown.

why.a: Wrong, and it is the opposite: the whole system is a single process, so no sub-processes appear.
why.b: Wrong. The context diagram comes FIRST and defines the scope the lower levels decompose.
why.c: Correct. Stores are excluded unless owned elsewhere.
why.d: Wrong. Internal stores are hidden at this level.

prompt: Match each actor in the bank generalisation example with its correct role.

pairs.right: The abstract actor representing any person who uses the banking system and can make deposits or withdrawals
A specialised customer type that inherits Customer use cases such as Make Deposit and Withdraw Money
A specialised customer type that inherits Customer use cases but may also access Request Overdraft

explanation: Generalisation between actors works exactly like inheritance. CUSTOMER is the abstract parent holding everything common. Both account holders inherit those use cases, and the current account holder adds one of its own, Request Overdraft, which the savings holder does not get. Draw the shared behaviour once on the parent and only the differences on the children.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the outcome for an analyst who violates fact-finding ethics by misusing sensitive information gathered during a project?

options.text: The project's requirements definition document becomes legally void
The organisation is required to restart the entire systems development life cycle from the planning phase
The analyst risks losing the respect, credibility, and confidence of users and management, and both the analyst and organisation may face legal liability
The analyst automatically receives a formal promotion for demonstrating initiative

explanation: Two kinds of damage, and the professional one is listed first for a reason. An analyst works by being trusted with things people would not otherwise say, so losing respect, credibility and confidence ends the ability to do the job at all. The legal liability, falling on both the analyst and the organisation, comes on top of that.

why.a: Wrong. A breach of ethics does not void a document.
why.b: Wrong. Nothing forces a restart of the life cycle.
why.c: Correct. Lost trust and credibility, plus legal liability for analyst and organisation.
why.d: Wrong, and it is the joke option.

prompt: Match each illegal data flow with the correction required to fix it.

pairs.left: Data flowing directly from one data store to another
pairs.right: A process must be inserted to move data from one data store to another

pairs.left: Data flowing directly from one external agent to another
pairs.right: A process must be inserted to exchange the data flow between the two boundaries

pairs.left: Data flowing directly from a data store to an external agent
pairs.right: A process must be inserted to present or retrieve the data from the store on the agent's behalf

explanation: One rule generates all three corrections: EVERY data flow must touch a process. So whenever two non-process symbols are joined directly, the fix is always the same, insert a process. Only the wording of what that process does changes: it MOVES data between stores, EXCHANGES data between agents, or RETRIEVES and PRESENTS data from a store to an agent.

prompt: An analyst is observing a warehouse clerk to understand how order picking really happens. Which two of the following are recommended guidelines for conducting this observation effectively?

options.text: Focus primarily on trivial, one-off activities to capture edge cases
Keep a low profile so the worker's normal behaviour is not disrupted
Obtain permission from the appropriate supervisor before observing
Interrupt the worker regularly to ask clarifying questions in real time

explanation: Observation exists to see what people ACTUALLY do rather than what they say they do, and both correct answers protect that. Keeping a low profile limits the effect of being watched, and getting the supervisor's permission first keeps the exercise authorised and stops it disrupting operations.

why.a: Wrong. Trivial one-off activities are the least representative thing you could watch.
why.b: Correct. A low profile keeps behaviour normal.
why.c: Correct. Permission first, from the appropriate supervisor.
why.d: Wrong, and it destroys the point: interrupting changes the very workflow you came to see.

prompt: Match each DFD error type with its correct description.

pairs.right: A process has outputs but no inputs, so data is produced from nothing
A process's inputs are insufficient to logically produce its stated outputs
A process has inputs but no outputs, so data enters and then disappears

explanation: Three failures, and the names are pictures. A BLACK HOLE swallows: data goes in, nothing comes out. A MIRACLE creates: output appears with no input to explain it. A GRAY HOLE is the subtle one, because it has both inputs and outputs, but the inputs could not possibly produce those outputs. Gray holes are the commonest real fault and the hardest to spot.

prompt: Which of the following data flows would be considered illegal according to standard DFD construction rules?

options.text: A data flow moving from an external entity into a process
A data flow moving from a process into a data store
A data flow moving directly from one data store to another data store without passing through a process
A data flow moving from a data store into a process

explanation: Read the four options and notice that three of them touch a process. That is the whole rule: a legal flow always has a process at one end. Store to store has no process anywhere, so nothing is doing the moving, and the flow is illegal.

why.a: Legal. An external entity supplying a process is the normal way data enters the system.
why.b: Legal. A process writing to a store is how data comes to rest.
why.c: Correct, this is the illegal one. No process at either end.
why.d: Legal. A process reading from a store is routine.

prompt: Which two of the following statements about Data Flow Diagrams are accurate?

options.text: DFDs are purely logical models that contain no implementation details
A system may have multiple Level 0 DFDs, one for each department
DFDs must specify the exact programming language used to implement each process
There can be only one Level 0 DFD for a given system

explanation: Both correct statements protect the same idea: a DFD describes ONE system, logically. Purely logical means no language, no hardware, no database product. Only one Level 0 means there is a single agreed top-level view of the whole system, which every lower level then decomposes. Allow two Level 0 diagrams and you no longer have one system, you have two.

why.a: Correct. Logical, with implementation deliberately excluded.
why.b: Wrong. Departments are not systems; one system gets one Level 0.
why.c: Wrong, and it contradicts the first correct answer.
why.d: Correct. Exactly one Level 0 for a given system.

prompt: Match each association notation with its correct meaning.

pairs.left: Association with an arrowhead touching the use case
pairs.right: Indicates the use case was initiated by the actor at the other end of the line
A line connecting an actor directly to a use case, representing participation in that use case
Indicates an interaction between the use case and an external server or receiver actor

explanation: The arrowhead carries the meaning, and it points at what was STARTED. An arrow touching the use case says the actor at the far end initiated it, which is what a primary actor does. No arrowhead means the actor was involved without starting anything, which is what an external server or receiver actor does. The plain line is simply participation.

prompt: Match each type of actor with its definition.

pairs.right: Benefits from the execution of the use case by receiving something of measurable or observable value
Directly interfaces with the system to initiate or trigger a business event
Responds to a request from the use case
Receives something of measurable or observable value (output) from the use case but is not the primary actor

explanation:
Split them on two questions. Is the actor PRIMARY or EXTERNAL, that is does it drive the use case or serve it? And does it GIVE or RECEIVE? The primary business actor benefits, the primary system actor touches the system and triggers the event, the external server responds when asked, and the external receiver gets an output without being the reason the use case ran.

Watch the pair that catches people: primary BUSINESS actor benefits from the outcome, primary SYSTEM actor is the one physically interacting with the system. They are often different people, such as a customer who benefits and a clerk who types.

prompt: Match each observation guideline with its underlying rationale.

pairs.left: Do not interrupt individuals while they are working
pairs.right: Avoids disrupting the natural workflow being studied

pairs.left: Take notes during or immediately following the observation
pairs.right: Preserves accurate detail before memory of the activity fades

pairs.left: Obtain permission from the appropriate supervisor before observing
pairs.right: Ensures the observation is authorised and does not improperly disrupt operations

pairs.left: Keep a low profile during the observation
pairs.right: Reduces the likelihood that the worker alters normal behaviour because they feel watched

explanation: Three of the four defend the same thing: seeing the work as it really is. Not interrupting protects the workflow, keeping a low profile protects the behaviour, and permission protects the operation. Only the note-taking rule is about YOU rather than them, and it exists because detail fades fast once you leave the room.

prompt: Which two of the following are legitimate reasons for conducting an interview during fact-finding?

options.text: To solicit ideas and opinions from stakeholders
To verify facts already gathered through other techniques
To automatically resolve all conflicting stakeholder requirements without further analysis
To eliminate the need for any written requirements documentation

explanation: Interviews do two jobs that no document can. They gather ideas and OPINIONS, which only exist in people's heads, and they VERIFY what you learned elsewhere, because a document tells you what the process is supposed to be while a person tells you what it actually is. Both wrong options overclaim: interviewing neither settles conflicts by itself nor removes the need to write anything down.

why.a: Correct. Ideas and opinions come from people.
why.b: Correct. Verifying facts gathered by other means is a standard purpose.
why.c: Wrong. Conflicts surface in interviews; resolving them takes analysis and negotiation.
why.d: Wrong. What is said still has to be documented, or it is lost.

prompt: A process named "Add 1 to the counter" is considered problematic in DFD naming conventions primarily because it is which of the following?

options.text: Named using a noun rather than a verb
Procedural, describing how a step is implemented rather than what business function is performed
Missing a corresponding data store
Insufficiently detailed for a programmer to implement

explanation: This is the logical-model rule biting at the level of a single label. "Add 1 to the counter" is a line of code, not a business function. A DFD process should be named for what the BUSINESS does, in a verb plus object form such as Record Payment or Validate Order. If the name would still make sense to someone who has never seen a computer, it is at the right level.

why.a: Wrong, and it is the tempting one: the name does start with a verb, Add. The fault is not grammar, it is level.
why.b: Correct. It describes implementation rather than business function.
why.c: Wrong. Not every process needs a data store.
why.d: Wrong, and backwards: the problem is that it is too implementation-specific, not too vague.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the relationship between a Level 0 DFD and a Level 1 DFD in the same process model?

options.text: A Level 1 DFD must contain fewer data flows than the Context Diagram
A Level 1 DFD replaces the need for a Context Diagram entirely
A Level 1 DFD always precedes and determines the structure of the Level 0 DFD
A Level 1 DFD further decomposes one specific process from the Level 0 DFD into more detailed sub-processes, while conserving that process's original inputs and outputs

explanation: Two ideas in one sentence, and both carry marks. DECOMPOSITION: a Level 1 diagram explodes ONE process from Level 0, not the whole diagram. CONSERVATION: the inputs and outputs of that parent process must all still be there, which is balancing. Levelling without balancing produces a set of diagrams that quietly contradict each other.

why.a: Wrong, and usually the reverse: decomposing reveals MORE detail, not less.
why.b: Wrong. The context diagram sets the boundary and stays.
why.c: Wrong direction. Level 0 comes first and Level 1 decomposes part of it.
why.d: Correct. One process decomposed, with its inputs and outputs conserved.

prompt: Which two of the following are documented consequences of incorrect system requirements?

options.text: The system will automatically pass all user acceptance testing
The system may be delivered later than promised
The system may cost more than originally projected
The system's data flows will automatically balance across all decomposition levels

explanation: The same two consequences the manual gives on page 7 and repeats in Module One: LATE and OVER BUDGET, alongside a system that does not solve the problem. The reason is that a requirements error is discovered last, after the design, the code and the data structures have all been built on it, so fixing it means unpicking everything above it.

why.a: Wrong, and it is the opposite: wrong requirements are what acceptance testing exists to catch.
why.b: Correct. Late delivery is one of the named consequences.
why.c: Correct. Cost overrun is the other.
why.d: Wrong. Balancing is a property of how you DRAW the diagrams, unrelated to requirement quality.

prompt: Which two outputs are produced when performing use-case modelling?

options.text: The use-case narrative
The entity-relationship diagram
The use-case diagram
The Gantt chart

explanation: Use-case modelling always produces a PAIR, and marks are lost by naming only one. The DIAGRAM is the picture: actors, use cases, and the lines between them, showing scope at a glance. The NARRATIVE is the text behind each use case: preconditions, main flow, alternative flows, postconditions. The diagram shows what exists; the narrative says what happens.

why.a: Correct. The narrative is the written half.
why.b: Wrong. An ERD is the output of DATA modelling, not use-case modelling.
why.c: Correct. The diagram is the visual half.
why.d: Wrong. A Gantt chart is a project scheduling tool.

prompt: Match each term with its correct definition.

pairs.right: A collection of activities designed to produce a specific output for a particular customer or market
A specific ordering of work activities across time and place, with a beginning, an end, and defined inputs and outputs
A technique for organising and documenting a system's processes, inputs, outputs, and data stores
A pictorial representation of reality

explanation:
Two of these look interchangeable and are not, so take them in the manual's own words.

A BUSINESS PROCESS is a collection of activities producing a specific output for a particular customer or market. Its emphasis is on HOW work is done in an organisation, in contrast to a product, which is about what. Making lunch is the example: the output is the lunch, and the activities inside it are the processes.

A PROCESS is narrower and more precisely shaped: a specific ordering of work activities across time and place, with a beginning, an end, and clearly defined inputs and outputs. The manual calls it a structure for action. Assemble sandwich ingredients is a process; making lunch is the business process containing it.

A MODEL is a pictorial representation of reality, and PROCESS MODELLING is the technique for organising and documenting a system's processes, inputs, outputs and data stores, whose main tool is the Data Flow Diagram.

The short version: the business process is the WHOLE job for a customer, the process is one ordered step inside it with a beginning and an end.

prompt: Match each banking use case with its correct relationship description.

pairs.right: Depends on Open account being performed first
Depends on Make deposit being performed first
An inherited use case available to both Savings Account Holder and Current Account Holder via generalisation
Depicted in the example as an additional use case specific to the Current Account Holder

explanation:
Two different relationships are being tested at once, which is what makes this hard.

The first two are DEPENDS ON, and the manual gives the chain on page 62: withdrawing cash depends on first depositing cash, and depositing cash depends on opening a bank account. Read it as an order in time, because a depends-on relationship says one use case cannot happen until another has.

The last two are GENERALISATION. Customer is the abstract parent, so Withdraw Money and Check Balance are inherited by BOTH account holders. Request Overdraft belongs only to the Current Account Holder, because it is the extra use case that specialisation adds.

So: depends-on is about ORDER, generalisation is about INHERITANCE. If a description mentions one being performed first, it is depends-on; if it mentions who has access, it is generalisation.
